opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the first version of FourCastNet used Fourier neural operators in a fairly direct way, and the Fourier transform implicitly assumes your domain is flat and periodic, like a torus or a rectangle that wraps around. That's a convenient approximation, and it got us surprisingly far. We were competitive with traditional numerical weather models at a tiny fraction of the cost, which was a big deal at the time.

But the Earth isn't a flat rectangle, it's a sphere. When you take a latitude-longitude grid and treat it as a flat image, you get distortions, especially near the poles. Grid points bunch up there, the geometry is stretched, and the model has to spend effort learning around those artifacts instead of learning the physics. For short-range forecasts you can get away with it. But once you roll the model out autoregressively over longer horizons, weeks or even longer for climate-type simulations, those small errors accumulate. We saw instabilities, artifacts blowing up near the poles, and energy not being conserved properly, so the rollouts would eventually drift into something unphysical.

So for the next version, the spherical Fourier neural operator, we replaced the standard Fourier transform with spherical harmonics, which are the natural basis functions on the sphere. That respects the geometry and the symmetries of the problem. Rotations on the sphere are handled properly, there's no artificial seam or pole singularity, and the model's inductive bias matches the real domain. The result was much more stable long rollouts. We could run it for a year or more and it stayed physically sensible, which opens the door to things like large ensembles and climate-scale studies.

And the broader lesson, which I keep coming back to, is that neural operators are powerful because they work in function space and are resolution-independent, but you still want to bring in the right domain knowledge. Respecting geometry, symmetries, and conservation properties isn't a constraint that hurts you. It's what lets these models generalize and stay stable where purely data-driven approaches would fall apart.

r001.rationale: It explains that treating Earth’s latitude–longitude grid as a flat image distorts the geometry, especially near the poles.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the first version of FourCastNet was built on the Adaptive Fourier Neural Operator, and we were honestly a bit surprised at how well it worked. It was something like tens of thousands of times faster than the numerical weather models and competitive on short lead times. But when you look under the hood, we were treating the Earth as a flat rectangle. We took the lat-lon grid, laid it out as a 2D image, and did standard FFTs on it. And that is just wrong as a prior, because the planet is a sphere.

What goes wrong is a few things. Near the poles, the grid points get squeezed together, so the model sees enormous distortion there, and the periodicity in longitude is fine but you have these artificial boundaries at the top and bottom that don't exist physically. Information that should flow smoothly over the pole gets cut off. The result is that errors accumulate in those regions, and when you autoregressively roll the model out, those errors feed back into the next step. So the first version was quite good for a few days, but when you tried to go out to a week or two, things would start to blow up or produce unphysical artifacts.

The more principled fix was to replace the Fourier transform with the spherical harmonic transform. That's what became the Spherical Fourier Neural Operator, which Boris Bonev and the NVIDIA team led. Spherical harmonics are the natural basis functions on the sphere, the same way sines and cosines are on a periodic domain. So the convolution in the neural operator becomes rotationally equivariant in the right way, and you respect the geometry by construction rather than hoping the network learns to compensate.

And the payoff was dramatic. We could run stable rollouts for a year or more, with the model staying physically plausible, which the flat version could never do. So it's a nice example of a theme I keep coming back to: when you build in the right structure, whether that's the operator learning framework itself or the geometry of the domain, you get better generalization and stability almost for free, instead of trying to brute-force it with data and parameters.

r001.rationale: The response explains that treating Earth as a flat rectangle misrepresents its spherical geometry, causing distortion near the poles and artificial boundaries.

astra-6.text:
The Earth is a sphere, and that geometry matters when you’re modeling global weather. If you represent it as a flat grid, you introduce distortions, especially near the poles. In the first version, the Fourier representation effectively treated the domain as flat and periodic, so it didn’t fully respect that geometry.

Moving to spherical harmonics lets us represent the dynamics on the sphere more naturally. That gives the model a better inductive bias: it can learn the weather patterns without also having to compensate for artifacts of the coordinate system. That’s especially important when you roll the model forward over many steps, because small errors can accumulate and affect the stability of the forecast.

r001.rationale: The response says a flat-grid representation introduces distortions, especially near the poles, and that the first version treated the domain as flat rather than respecting Earth's spherical geometry.

sol-6.1.text:
The first version of FourCastNet treated the latitude–longitude grid essentially as a flat image. But the Earth is a sphere, and that grid becomes highly distorted near the poles. Points that look far apart on the grid can actually be very close together geographically.

So incorporating spherical geometry gives the model the right inductive bias: it can represent spatial relationships and atmospheric dynamics on the actual domain where they occur. That becomes particularly important when you roll forecasts forward, because small errors can accumulate. We wanted the model to learn the weather dynamics without also having to learn around artifacts of the coordinate system.
